text: Section one, principle one. One forgotten command breaks the page. Every new element means one more command. Let's go back to the subscribe button for a moment. Suppose the page also has a short note under the button. It says, "Get one email a week," and that note should go away after the click. In the plain version, the note gets its own ID in the HTML. Our script finds it with document.getElementById and keeps it in a variable called note, the same way it found the button. Then the click handler needs a third command. The plain script again, subscribe.js. Line five hands the button a click listener, a small arrow function. Inside it, line six sets button.disabled to true. Line seven takes the class hidden off the thanks line, and line eight is the new one, note.classlist.addhidden. The note on that line says it plainly, "New command three, hide the note." Line nine just closes the function. In the React version, the handler stays exactly as it was. Only the JSX gets one more piece, a piece that reads done. What changed in subscribe.jsx? Look at line seven first. The button still has disabled equals done, and on click it calls setDone with true. The note there says the handler did not change. Line eight is new. In curly braces, an exclamation mark, done, the double ampersand, and then a paragraph with "Get one email a week." Its note says, "Shown only while done is false." Line nine is the old one, done, the double ampersand, thanks. And lines six and ten are the empty fragment tags wrapped around it all. The exclamation mark in front of done means not. At the start, done is false, so not done is true, and the note shows. After the click, done becomes true. Then not done is false, and the note goes away. So each new element costs the plain handler one more command. It costs the React handler nothing. With one click and two looks, the plain version is still easy to keep right. Now, let's build the promo code box, which has five looks. The fake server, a function that answers later. Before we write the plain page, we need our fake server. It lives in its own file. This file is checkcode.js in the src folder. Line one exports a function called checkCode, and it takes a code. Line two returns a new promise, which gets resolve and reject. The note says, "An answer that is not here yet." Line three starts a setTimeout. Line four asks, "Is the code exactly welcome?" If it is, line five calls resolve. The answer is yes. Otherwise, line seven calls reject with a new error that says, "This code is not valid." The answer is no. And on line nine, the number fifteen hundred tells setTimeout how long to wait. Lines ten and eleven close everything up. A real server does not answer right away. Its answer comes back a moment later. JavaScript has an object for exactly this case. It's called a promise. A promise is a JavaScript object that stands for an answer that is not here yet. Think of a burger counter that gives you a buzzer when you order. You get the buzzer right away, but the burger comes later. When the buzzer goes off, it tells you one of two things. Your order is ready, or sorry, we're sold out. A promise is that buzzer. When JavaScript creates a new promise, it calls the small function we pass in. It hands that function two other functions, resolve and reject. Calling resolve means the answer is yes. Calling reject means the answer is no. The three equal signs, in code three equal signs, welcome, asks JavaScript whether two values are exactly the same. The answer is true or false. Here is what checkCode does step by step. First, it returns a new promise right away. The answer is not known yet. Then, inside the promise, setTimeout waits fifteen hundred milliseconds, which is one and a half seconds. If the code is exactly welcome, it calls resolve. The answer is yes. Otherwise, it calls reject. The answer is no. We pass reject a new error, which is a standard JavaScript error object. Ours carries the message, "This code is not valid." The plain promo page. Now, the plain page, the HTML loads our style sheet and holds the whole form. Every element has an ID, so our script can find it. Ten lines in plain.html. Line one links our style sheet, index.css, from the source folder. Line two opens a form with the ID promoForm, and line three is its heading, promoCode. Line four is the input box, codeInput. Line five is the apply button, applyButton, and notice the word disabled sitting on it. Line six is the checking line with the class hidden. Line seven closes the form. Then outside the form, line eight is the error line with two classes, error and hidden, and the text, "This code is not valid." Line nine is the success line, also hidden. It says, "Code applied. You get free delivery." And line ten loads our script, plainpromo.js, as a module. In HTML, writing disabled on a tag turns the element off from the start. It's the same switch as the disabled property our script can set. So the apply button starts off because the box starts empty. The checking line, the error line, and the success line all start with the class hidden. The error line also has the class error, which our style sheet colors red. The error line and the success line sit outside the form. There's a reason for that. After a success, we will hide the whole form. If the success line were inside the form, it would hide, too. The script starts by finding every element it will change. Line one brings in check code imported from checkcode.js. Line two is empty. Then lines three to eight all do the same thing six times. Each one calls document.getElementById and keeps what it finds in a const. Form gets promo form, code input gets code input, apply button gets apply button, checking text gets checking, error text gets error, and success text gets success. Each of these six names is our own variable. Each one holds one element of the page found by the ID we wrote in the HTML. While the shopper types, the apply button should work only when the box has text. Just three lines this time, ten to twelve. Line ten gives code input a listener for the input event. Line eleven is the highlighted one. Applybutton.disabled gets codeinput.value.length three equal signs zero. The note says, "Off while the box is empty." Line twelve closes it. The browser fires the input event on every keystroke, and it calls our small function each time. Inside it, codeinput.value is the text in the box right now. Its length is the number of letters in that text. The highlighted line looks dense, so here it is in order. JavaScript reads the text in the box and counts its letters. Next, it checks whether that count is exactly zero. The answer is true or false, and it stores that answer in applybutton.disabled. So when the box is empty, the answer is true and the button is off. As soon as the box holds one letter, the answer is false and the button works.
